# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is useful for teams currently using Slack who are considering switching to Element, possibly due to concerns over data ownership or cost. The core use case for both tools is team communication and collaboration, and someone might switch to gain more control over their data or to reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Element allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, while Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup Complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, especially for self-hosting, while Slack is generally easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Slack has better support for large teams and enterprises, while Element can be more challenging to scale.
* Feature Difference: Element has end-to-end encryption for all conversations, while Slack only offers this feature for certain paid plans.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations with other tools and services
* Good support for large teams and enterprises
* Mobile apps for on-the-go access
* Limited control over data and limited end-to-end encryption
### Element
* Free and self-hosted, giving teams full control over their data
* End-to-end encryption for all conversations
* Customizable and extensible with a wide range of plugins and integrations
* Can be more challenging to set up and maintain, especially for non-technical teams
* Limited support for large teams and enterprises

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams who need a simple, easy-to-use communication platform with a wide range of integrations and good support for large teams and enterprises. It's also a good choice for teams who don't need full control over their data and are willing to pay for the convenience of a hosted solution. Element, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams who need full control over their data and want a self-hosted solution. It's also a good choice for teams who value end-to-end encryption and customization, and are willing to put in the time and effort to set up and maintain their own server.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which produces a JSON file containing all your team's messages, files, and other data.
2. Set up an Element server, either on your own hardware or using a cloud hosting provider.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data into your new Element server.
4. Configure your Element server and set up any necessary plugins or integrations.
5. Invite your team to join your new Element server and start using it for all your communication and collaboration needs.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, due to its limited support for large teams and enterprises, as well as its more complex setup and maintenance requirements. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element's scalability can be a challenge, requiring significant technical expertise to set up and maintain a large-scale deployment. We recommend switching to Element if you're a small to medium-sized team who values data control and customization, and is willing to put in the time and effort to set up and maintain your own server.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 20 users) who don't need a wide range of integrations and are looking for a free, self-hosted solution.
* Teams who value end-to-end encryption and data control, and are willing to put in the time and effort to set up and maintain their own server.
* Technical teams who are comfortable with complex setup and maintenance requirements, and want a customizable and extensible solution.
* Teams who don't need support for large teams and enterprises, and are looking for a simple, easy-to-use solution.
* Teams who are currently using Slack's free plan and are looking for a free, self-hosted alternative.

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted, giving teams full control over their data and saving them money on hosting costs.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element is more challenging to set up and maintain, especially for non-technical teams.
### Can I integrate Element with other tools and services?
Yes, Element has a wide range of plugins and integrations available, although it may not have as many as Slack.
### Is Element secure?
Yes, Element has end-to-end encryption for all conversations, giving teams full control over their data and ensuring that it remains secure.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data using the Slack export tool and import it into Element using the Element import tool.

title: Discord vs Element
comparison_markdown:
# Discord vs Element

## Overview

Chat platform popular with gaming and developer communities. is a popular proprietary tool in the communication space. Element is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Discord costs Free / $9.99/month; Element is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Discord is Proprietary; Element is Apache 2.0
- **Data ownership**: Element can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Element eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Element has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Discord

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Element

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [element-hq/element-web](https://github.com/element-hq/element-web) * ~11k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Discord if:** Discord is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Element if:** Element is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Discord in its standard export format, review Element import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Element is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Discord tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Element instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Discord, switching to self-hosted Element will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Discord until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Discord paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Element free to use?
Yes. Element is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Discord to Element?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Discord data, follow the Element import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Element get regular updates?
Yes. Element has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Element without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Element development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Discord](https://discord.com) and [Element](https://element.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Element is a free, self-hosted alternative to Discord. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: GitHub vs GitLab
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs GitLab

## Overview

GitHub is the world largest code hosting platform, owned by Microsoft, with 100 million developers. GitLab is a complete DevOps platform that can be fully self-hosted, offering everything from Git hosting to CI/CD and container registries.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub free tier is generous; GitLab Community Edition is fully free to self-host
- **CI/CD**: GitLab has more powerful built-in CI/CD pipelines; GitHub Actions is catching up
- **Self-hosting**: GitLab is designed to be self-hosted; GitHub Enterprise self-hosted is expensive
- **Feature scope**: GitLab is a complete DevSecOps platform; GitHub focuses on developer collaboration
- **Community**: GitHub has a dramatically larger open-source community and project discoverability

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### GitLab

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [gitlabhq/gitlabhq](https://github.com/gitlabhq/gitlabhq) * ~24k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub suits open-source projects wanting maximum community visibility or teams deeply integrated with GitHub Actions workflows.

**Choose GitLab if:** GitLab self-hosted is ideal for enterprises needing full control over their DevOps stack or regulated industries.

## Migration Path

GitLab provides a GitHub importer that migrates repositories, issues, PRs, wikis, and milestones. Update CI configuration from GitHub Actions to GitLab CI/CD YAML format.

## Our Take

GitLab is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your GitLab instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted GitLab will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is GitLab free to use?
Yes. GitLab is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to GitLab?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the GitLab import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does GitLab get regular updates?
Yes. GitLab has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use GitLab without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if GitLab development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [GitLab](https://gitlab.com) before making decisions.*
meta_description: GitLab is a free, self-hosted alternative to GitHub. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are both design and prototyping tools used by product teams, designers, and developers. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering a switch from Figma to Penpot, particularly those prioritizing data ownership and cost-effectiveness. The core use case for both tools is user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) design, with the key reason to switch being the desire for a free or self-hosted solution.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Penpot is completely free and open-source.
* Data Ownership: Penpot allows users to self-host and have full control over their data, whereas Figma stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup Complexity: Figma has a more straightforward setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Figma is designed for large teams and enterprises, while Penpot is more suitable for small to medium-sized teams.
* Feature Difference: Figma has a more comprehensive set of features, including advanced prototyping and collaboration tools, while Penpot has a stronger focus on design systems and open-source community involvement.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Comprehensive set of features for design, prototyping, and collaboration
* Large community of users and developers
* Well-established and reliable platform
* Integrates with many third-party tools and services
* Offers a free plan with limited features
### Penpot
* Completely free and open-source
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Strong focus on design systems and open-source community involvement
* Customizable and extensible through plugins and APIs
* Limited features compared to Figma, particularly in prototyping and collaboration

## When to Choose Each
Figma is suitable for large teams and enterprises that require a comprehensive set of features, advanced prototyping, and collaboration tools. It is also a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a well-established platform. Penpot, on the other hand, is ideal for small to medium-sized teams, startups, or individuals who prioritize data ownership, cost-effectiveness, and customization. It is also a good choice for teams that are already familiar with open-source tools and have the technical expertise for self-hosting.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to upload your designs to Penpot.
3. Configure your Penpot instance, including setting up user accounts and permissions.
4. Update your design files to take advantage of Penpot's features and plugins.
5. Test and refine your designs in Penpot to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Penpot is not yet production-ready for most users, as it lacks some of the features and polish of Figma. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's collaboration features are still in development and may not be as robust as Figma's. However, for teams that prioritize data ownership and cost-effectiveness, Penpot is a viable alternative, and we recommend switching to Penpot if you are a small to medium-sized team with basic design needs.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need advanced prototyping features
* Startups or individuals who prioritize cost-effectiveness and data ownership
* Teams that are already familiar with open-source tools and have the technical expertise for self-hosting
* Designers who work on simple UI/UX projects and do not require advanced collaboration features
* Educational institutions or non-profit organizations that need a free or low-cost design solution

### Can I use Penpot for free?
Yes, Penpot is completely free and open-source, with no costs or licensing fees.

No, Penpot is more suitable for small to medium-sized teams, as it lacks some of the features and scalability of Figma.

Yes, Penpot has a growing ecosystem of integrations and plugins, although it may not be as comprehensive as Figma's.
